title: Check yourself: what the host actually receives

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A client runs on a server in Sydney, which is 11 hours ahead of GMT in January. It sets field 7 with ISODate.getDateTime(new Date()). A purchase leaves at 09:00 Sydney time on 20 January. What does the host find in field 7?

options.text: 0119220000, since getDateTime formats the instant in GMT unless told otherwise
options.says: the one-argument getDateTime formats in the JVM's default zone, here Sydney

options.text: 0120090000, since getDateTime formats the instant in the JVM's default zone
options.says: without a zone argument the helper uses the default zone, so the host reads Sydney time as GMT, 11 hours off

options.text: 0119220000, since the packager converts field 7 to GMT when it packs the message
options.says: the packager only pads and checks length; it never interprets the value

options.text: 0120090000, since the packager sends field 7 in the terminal's own local time
options.says: the packager sends the string it was given; the local time comes from the helper, not the packager

origin.section: 2.4 Field 7 Is GMT, Whatever the Server's Time Zone

questions.stem: When a client sends a purchase it saves a row keyed by the request's field 11, and when the response comes it looks the row up by the response's field 11. One purchase was built with m.set(11, "4096") and sent with the iso87ascii packager. The host approves it, sending field 11 back in its response. What does the lookup return?

options.text: The saved row, since QMUX pads the request's field 11 when it matches the response
options.says: QMUX pads a copy of the value for its key; the request's field 11 and the saved row still say 4096

options.text: Nothing, since the host gives each response a trace number of its own choosing
options.says: the host echoes the request's field 11; it does not number its responses itself

options.text: The saved row, since the packager pads the value inside the ISOMsg as well
options.says: the packager pads only the bytes it writes; getString(11) on the request still returns 4096

options.text: Nothing, since the host sends back the six digits that the packager wrote
options.says: the wire carried 004096, so the response says 004096 while the row is keyed by 4096

origin.section: 2.1 An ISOMsg Holds Strings, and the Packager Decides the Bytes

questions.stem: To avoid keeping a counter, a developer sets field 11 to the time of day as HHmmss. Field 41 is the same on every request, and at busy times the link carries four requests per second, each answered within two seconds. What do you expect to see at busy times?

options.text: Requests started in the same second share a STAN, so QMUX refuses all but one of them
options.says: with field 41 constant the key is the STAN, and only one request per key can wait

options.text: Requests started in the same second share a STAN, but QMUX tells them apart by amount
options.says: the default key is fields 41 and 11; the amount is not part of it

options.text: Every request has a STAN of its own, since field 7 is part of the key QMUX builds
options.says: field 7 is not a key field; requests in one second get the same HHmmss

options.text: Every request has a STAN of its own, since the packager puts the date before field 11
options.says: the packager writes field 11 as six digits and adds nothing to it

origin.section: 2.5 The STAN Is One Sequence per Link

questions.stem: To keep card numbers out of the logs, a developer adds m.set(2, ISOUtil.protect(m.getString(2))) before mux.request, and logs each request with m.dump. What becomes of the purchases?

options.text: The log is masked and they are approved, since the channel puts the clear number back before sending
options.says: the channel sends field 2 as it is; nothing in jPOS keeps the clear number

options.text: The log shows clear numbers and they are approved, since dump prints field 2 as first set
options.says: set replaced field 2; dump prints the current, masked value

options.text: The log is masked and they are declined, since the host receives the masked number in field 2
options.says: protect's result replaced the PAN in the message, so the host gets a card number that does not exist

options.text: The log shows clear numbers and they are declined, since protect leaves field 2 alone
options.says: protect returns a copy, but set then stores that copy in field 2

origin.section: 2.6 Mask What You Print, Never What You Send

questions.stem: A client uses a ChannelAdaptor with its default settings. A purchase is waiting for its answer when another purchase, with nine characters in field 41, is handed to the same MUX. The host would answer both within a second. What do the two callers of request see?

options.text: The second gets an ISOException at once and the first gets its answer, since the MUX packs before queueing
options.says: the MUX only queues the message; the channel packs it on its own thread

options.text: Both get null when their timeouts run out, since the adaptor closes the link when the pack fails
options.says: in 2.1.7 the sender disconnects on an ISOException, so the first answer is lost and the second message was never sent

options.text: The second gets an ISOException at once and the first gets null, since the failed pack stops the reader
options.says: the pack error is only logged by the adaptor; the caller of request just waits

options.text: Both get null when their timeouts run out, since the host rejects the message and drops the link
options.says: the bad message never reaches the host; the client's own adaptor closes the link

origin.section: 2.2 A Message That Doesn't Pack Fails on the Channel Thread

concepts: Masking is applied to what is printed or logged; the message keeps the real PAN, and dump prints it in clear.
An ISOMsg keeps the strings it was given; the packager pads short values and refuses long ones only when it packs, so a short STAN in memory differs from the one the host echoes.
